blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the concept of 'capsules' in neural networks, highlighting their potential to address exponential inefficiencies in traditional models like HMMs and CNNs. The key insight is that capsules encode viewpoint-invariant knowledge using transformation matrices, allowing for better generalization to novel viewpoints. The blog post explains that capsules represent entities and their properties (e.g., pose, deformation) as vectors, with the vector length indicating the existence of the entity and orientation encoding its properties. A dynamic routing mechanism ensures that capsules in lower layers send their outputs to appropriate parent capsules in higher layers based on agreement, improving upon the crude max-pooling approach in CNNs. The paper demonstrates these ideas on the MNIST dataset, showing how capsules can learn meaningful representations of digit variations.
paper_abstract: A capsule is a group of neurons whose activity vector represents the instantiation parameters of a specific type of entity such as an object or an object part. We use the length of the activity vector to represent the probability that the entity exists and its orientation to represent the instantiation parameters. Active capsules at one level make predictions, via transformation matrices, for the instantiation parameters of higher-level capsules. When multiple predictions agree, a higher level capsule becomes active. We show that a discrimininatively trained, multi-layer capsule system achieves state-of-the-art performance on MNIST and is considerably better than a convolutional net at recognizing highly overlapping digits. To achieve these results we use an iterative routing-by-agreement mechanism: A lower-level capsule prefers to send its output to higher level capsules whose activity vectors have a big scalar product with the prediction coming from the lower-level capsule.
